title: Callano v. Oakwood Park Homes Corp.
lead: Julia and Frank Callano planted shrubbery for a prospective homebuyer who died without paying. When the developer later retained and resold the improved property, the nursery sought restitution from the developer, but the appellate court held that these facts did not justify replacing the nursery’s chosen contractual debtor.

actors.name: Bruce Pendergast
actors.role: Prospective homebuyer who ordered the landscaping and owed the invoice.

actors.name: Oakwood Park Homes Corporation
actors.role: Developer that retained and resold the improved property.

actors.name: Judge Collester
actors.role: Author of the unanimous appellate opinion.

proceedings: Trial court awarded $475 on stipulated facts under quasi-contract. New Jersey Appellate Division reversed; no judgment was entered against Pendergast’s estate in this action.
limits: The invoice was $497.95; the stipulated enhancement was $475. The opinion does not report the estate’s solvency or any later collection. Its conclusion concerns the particular dealings, not a universal bar to supplier restitution.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The nursery contracts with the prospective buyer
sections.cue: The developer knows about planting but does not order it.
paragraphs: Oakwood Park Homes Corporation was building a housing development. In December 1961 it contracted to sell Bruce Pendergast a lot and a house to be built there. Before construction was complete, nursery operators Julia and Frank Callano contracted with Pendergast to supply and plant shrubbery. Pendergast was their customer and the person from whom they expected payment.

The Callanos delivered and planted the shrubbery in May 1962. An Oakwood representative knew the planting was occurring. Pendergast did not pay the $497.95 invoice and died shortly afterward. On July 10, Oakwood and Pendergast’s estate canceled the real-estate contract. Oakwood did not know that the nursery remained unpaid. Six days later, Oakwood sold the property, including the shrubbery, to Richard and Joan Grantges. The resale price was not disclosed.

sections.title: The nursery recovers the improvement’s value at trial
sections.cue: A stipulated benefit leaves injustice as the disputed question.
paragraphs: The Callanos pursued Oakwood on a quasi-contractual theory: the developer had retained the improvement after cancellation and then sold the improved property. The case was tried on agreed facts. The parties stipulated that the shrubbery enhanced the property’s value by $475, an amount distinct from the invoice. The trial court entered judgment for that $475.

Oakwood appealed. The record did not contain a jury finding that Oakwood had requested the landscaping or promised to pay. The question was whether retention of the conceded benefit nevertheless created a legally imposed obligation to compensate the nursery.

sections.title: The appellate court separates benefit from unjust retention
sections.cue: Quasi-contract requires a reason to impose a duty on this recipient.
paragraphs: Judge Collester wrote for Judges Goldmann, Foley, and Collester. The court explained that an obligation implied by law differs from an express or implied-in-fact agreement. Quasi-contract imposes a remedial duty grounded in equity and justice without requiring actual assent. But the ability to identify someone who received value does not alone establish such a duty. The legal fiction must be used cautiously and requires circumstances making retention without payment unjust.

The Callanos therefore did not lose because the shrubbery lacked value, because value was uncertain, or because Oakwood received no benefit. Those matters were stipulated. Their difficulty was identifying an equitable reason why Oakwood, rather than Pendergast, should pay.

Successful quasi-contract claims commonly involved an expectation of payment from the defendant or an expectation that would have existed had the true facts been known. A direct relationship or a mistake could explain why a duty ran between those parties. Here the Callanos knowingly chose Pendergast as their contractual customer and expected him to pay. They had no relevant direct dealings with Oakwood and made no mistake about who ordered the work or owed the price.

sections.title: Later retention does not reallocate the original payment obligation
sections.cue: The contract claim against the estate remains distinct.
paragraphs: Oakwood’s knowledge that planting was occurring did not amount to an order. When it canceled the sale, Oakwood did not know the invoice was unpaid. The stipulated facts disclosed no plan to obtain free landscaping or shift Pendergast’s obligation onto the nursery. Absence of a promise was not automatically decisive in restitution, but nothing else here supplied the necessary equitable obligation.

The Callanos retained an express contractual claim arising from Pendergast’s undertaking. The court considered it inequitable on these facts to use quasi-contract merely to substitute a different debtor because that person ultimately enjoyed the improvement. Different dealings, mistake, an owner’s undertaking, or fraud could change the analysis; this record supplied none.

The nursery relied on De Gasperi v. Valicenti, a precedent allowing quasi-contractual recovery. The court distinguished it because the defendants there had perpetrated a fraud. No fraud by Oakwood was alleged, so that case did not make an innocent recipient automatically responsible for a third party’s unpaid contract.

The appellate court reversed the $475 judgment. Its reference to a remedy against Pendergast’s estate did not enter judgment against the estate, establish that the estate could pay, or show that the Callanos later collected. The reported panel issued no separate opinion.
